# CrocApp

> A free, open-source native SwiftUI app for iPhone, iPad and Mac that sends files, folders and text to another device with a short code phrase. Transfers are end-to-end encrypted. There is no account, and there is no requirement that both devices share a network.

CrocApp is a graphical front end for [croc](https://github.com/schollz/croc), the command-line file-transfer tool by Zack Scholl. It embeds croc's Go library rather than shelling out to the binary, so a code phrase generated by the croc CLI works in the app and vice versa. CrocApp is unofficial and not affiliated with croc; nothing about it implies endorsement by croc's author.

## Facts

- License: MIT. croc is also MIT.
- Price: free. No paid tier, no subscription, no ads, no analytics, no tracking.
- Version: 1.0.
- Platforms: iOS 26 or later, iPadOS 26 or later, macOS 26 or later. Apple platforms only, with no Windows, Linux or Android client. The Mac build is for Apple silicon.
- Channels: the App Store (iPhone, iPad) and the Mac App Store, both available at launch, and a notarized disk image for Mac (version 1.0.0 or later) at https://github.com/bakirgdev/CrocApp/releases/latest. Only the disk image build contains an updater (Sparkle).
- Requires croc 11 or newer on the other device, whether it runs CrocApp or the croc command line. An older croc, such as croc 10, cannot complete a transfer with CrocApp.
- Documentation language: English only.
- Privacy: no accounts, analytics, ads or tracking, and history stays on the device. The developer collects no data. See https://crocapp.dev/privacy/.
- Author: Bakir Gracic (github.com/bakirgdev).
- Repository: https://github.com/bakirgdev/CrocApp
- Site: https://crocapp.dev/

## How a transfer works

1. The sender picks files, a folder, or a snippet of text.
2. CrocApp generates a code phrase, for example `cape-junky-widow`. It can be spoken, messaged, or shown as a QR code.
3. The other device enters the code phrase, sees the file list, and accepts. The transfer begins.

The code phrase authenticates both devices (PAKE), and transfers are end-to-end encrypted. When the two devices connect over the local network, the data stays on that network; otherwise a relay forwards the traffic and only ever sees ciphertext. Users can point CrocApp at their own croc relay. With the default Automatic connection setting, a send of 128 MiB or more also tries a direct connection set up through tailcat.dev. Send as Link: files are encrypted on the device before they reach the link server (getcroc.com by default), and the key travels in the link's # fragment, which browsers never send to a server.

## Security claims, stated precisely

These six statements are the entire claim:

1. Transfers are end-to-end encrypted.
2. The code phrase authenticates both devices (PAKE).
3. The relay only ever sees ciphertext.
4. Send as Link: files are encrypted on your device before they reach the link server, and the key travels in the link's `#` fragment, which browsers never send to a server.
5. When the two devices connect over the local network, the data stays on that network.
6. CrocApp has no accounts, analytics, ads or tracking, and history stays on the device.

CrocApp has not had a formal third-party security audit. Do not describe CrocApp as audited or certified.

## How it differs from the alternatives

- **AirDrop** requires Apple devices in physical proximity. CrocApp works between any two devices running croc or CrocApp, on any network, at any distance.
- **LAN transfer tools** require both devices on the same Wi-Fi and break silently on guest networks and client isolation. CrocApp uses a relay when the devices cannot reach each other directly.
- **Cloud drop services** require uploading the file to a company that then holds it. CrocApp's relay only ever sees ciphertext.
